svg.title: Voltstream: how each injected fault is handled
svg.desc: Matrix of the six faults FaultInjector injects and one deliberate design choice, and how each layer handles them. raw-archiver writes every record unchanged. F1 null_field, F2 negative_kwh and F3 unknown_household are rejected by both layers: the speed layer writes them to rejected_records and meter.readings.dlq, the billing job to rejected_records only; they drive the HighRejectRate alert. F4 out-of-order readings within 30 simulated minutes are counted by both. F5 duplicates are removed by both on (meter_id, event_ts). F6 dropout backfill older than the 30-minute watermark is dropped by the speed layer but counted by the batch rescan, which is the data effect. T: the speed layer prices day D with the previous day's tariff, the batch layer with D's, which is the tariff effect. Reconciliation splits speed minus batch exactly into the two effects and pushes the mean percentage to voltstream_lambda_divergence, which drives LambdaDivergenceHigh.
svg.text: 4 · What happens to a bad, repeated or late reading
Rows are what FaultInjector does (rates from config/base.yaml) plus one deliberate staleness, T. Columns follow the reading through the pipeline.
2 %, on top of any other fault
speed prices D with tariff D−1;
day's batch rejects replaced per run;
the watermark is dropped → kWh low
S = speed estimate (tariff D−1) · B = batch final (tariff D) · C = speed kWh priced with tariff D, by core/tariff.py
